{"id": "2:24/q01", "question": "What action do the challengers fail to do?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q01/p1", "position": "Produce a surah comparable to the Qur'an, even with their helpers; they failed before and will fail thereafter.", "reasons": "Muqatil notes the fronted wording; al-Tabari includes testing and helpers, and Ibn Jurayj says summon witnesses to judge the match. Al-Tabrisi and Ibn Ashur include allies and consultation. Al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Qatada stress past failure and future inability; Elmalılı extends it to Resurrection."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q02", "question": "What makes the unanswered challenge evidence for revelation and prophethood?", "turns_on": "Whether the inability lies in the Qur'an's qualities or a divine diversion of the challengers.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q02/p1", "position": "The Qur'an itself surpasses opponents' ability, especially in its eloquent composition and other excellences.", "reasons": "Al-Rummani: strong motives would produce an answer if possible, and universal challenge makes silence decisive; sound harmony, clarity, and proof contribute. Al-Tabrisi uses rational inference. Al-Razi cites hostility, Muhammad's prudent refusal to risk disgrace, and no answer through his era. Ibn Kathir lists language, knowledge, true unseen reports and just rulings. Ibn Ashur stresses eloquence, style, wisdom, full-surah composition, continued transmission, and Arab and non-Arab access through testimony and learning; he rejects style alone, noncontradiction, or unseen reports alone as sufficient. Elmalılı treats the challenge as an experimentally checkable effect. Al-Walid and Bedouin reactions illustrate perceived eloquence."}, {"id": "2:24/q02/p2", "position": "God diverted challengers' desire or ability to answer (ṣarfah), itself an extraordinary sign.", "reasons": "Al-Rummani accepts it as one aspect beyond customary patterns. Ibn Ashur says a minority holds it; reports differ whether al-Ashari, al-Nazzam, al-Murtada, al-Isfarayini, Ibn Hazm, or many Mu'tazilites are counted. Ibn Ashur rejects the theory."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q03", "question": "What does the future prediction add to the proof?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q03/p1", "position": "It is a fulfilled prophecy of failure and thus knowledge of the unseen, strengthening the proof of prophethood.", "reasons": "Al-Rummani compares Badr, Roman recovery, ascendancy, and other predictions. Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan say it provokes efforts and makes failure more striking. Al-Zamakhshari, Baydawi, Nasafi and Alusi say an answer would have been transmitted. Razi and Baydawi say a false claimant would not risk so testable a prediction. Ibn Ashur says it holds across centuries; Elmalılı counts 1,344 years. Abu Hayyan distinguishes Musaylima and al-Mutanabbi's claims from a true counterchallenge."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q04", "question": "Why use conditional إن despite certainty of failure?", "turns_on": "Whether the condition adopts the opponents' outlook or expresses ironic certainty.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q04/p1", "position": "It speaks from the opponents' pre-reflection confidence or uncertainty, inviting a fair test while exposing their presumption.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari, Razi, Nasafi, Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Biqai, Burhan, Alusi, and Ibn Ashur say eloquent opponents expected a chance to succeed. Ibn Ashur says the apparent openness encourages attempt, exhausts excuses and alternates conciliation and threat."}, {"id": "2:24/q04/p2", "position": "It is a taunt or ironic condition from one certain of victory.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari and Razi compare a strong man saying 'if you defeat me'; Abu Hayyan, Baydawi and Alusi include mockery. Study Quran says a divine conditional need not imply uncertainty."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q05", "question": "How do إن and لم govern the first verb?", "turns_on": "Whether two particles with distinct meanings can compete for one verb.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q05/p1", "position": "إن conditions the whole negative clause; لم makes the imperfect jussive and past in sense.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Wahidi, Tabrisi, Baydawi and Ibn Ashur distinguish their functions. Nahhas, Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi say إن can precede past-like لم because it is non-governing in written form. Akhfash and Ibn Atiyya analogize لم to negative لا dropping an ending; others analogize it to conditional إن. Wahidi says conditional clauses' length favors deletion. Alusi leaves the exact syntactic locus unresolved; Samin makes the whole clause occupy the conditional's jussive place. Ibn Ashur rejects competing government here because meanings differ."}, {"id": "2:24/q05/p2", "position": "إن and لم compete to govern the same verb.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Alj allows particle competition; Ibn Hisham objects that particles do not denote events, and Alusi and Ibn Ashur object that these particles differ in polarity. Ibn Ashur notes Abu Ali al-Farisi allows competition when semantic demands agree and cites a rajaz example."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q06", "question": "Why say 'do it' instead of repeating the challenged act?", "turns_on": "Whether the challenge's object is grammatically omitted or the general verb is used absolutely.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q06/p1", "position": "The broad verb concisely stands for bringing a matching surah and its required conditions.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari, Baydawi, Nasafi, Burhan, Biqai, Alusi, Ibn Ashur and Samin invoke brevity. Biqai says denial of the broader act covers the specific one. Ibn Ashur includes witnesses. Abu Hayyan and the Sheikh object that 'bring' with omitted object could be just as concise. Samarai says omission leaves formal scope unrestricted."}, {"id": "2:24/q06/p2", "position": "The verb denotes simply performing the action; no grammatical object need be restored.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashi says transitive verbs can be used without an intended object when occurrence alone matters, comparing eat and drink; he also discusses how conditions and plurals compress alternatives and how fronting works."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q07", "question": "What does لن express, and how long does its negation last?", "turns_on": "Whether emphasis and duration are inherent in the particle or supplied by context.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q07/p1", "position": "It negates the future emphatically; any permanence here rests on the prediction or context, not the particle alone.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari, Razi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Suyuti and Abu Hayyan describe emphasis. Abu Hayyan says its overt future marking strengthens it; Burhan cites 19:26, 2:95, 20:91, 22:73 against inherent perpetuity. Alusi rejects fixed long or short duration; Samin denies inherent permanence."}, {"id": "2:24/q07/p2", "position": "It expresses an unbounded or permanent future negation, literally or by emphasis.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari cites 22:73 and this challenge. Ibn Ashur argues that unbounded future denial normally spans all future times and disputes grammarians who deny such force."}, {"id": "2:24/q07/p3", "position": "It denies an expected or near event without extending the negation indefinitely.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Zamalakani says لن denies something expected or near, whereas لا denies the doubtful; Abu Hayyan calls this nearly the reverse of Zamakhshari."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q08", "question": "What is the grammatical origin of لن?", "turns_on": "Whether the particle is primitive or derives from contracted or altered لا.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q08/p1", "position": "It is a simple, independent particle of future negation.", "reasons": "Wahidi cites object fronting before لن against a contracted relative particle; Sibawayh's objection is reported by Nahhas and Tabrisi. Abu Hayyan and Samin reject compound derivations. Ibn Ashur, however, calls Khalil's contraction good."}, {"id": "2:24/q08/p2", "position": "It contracts لا أن.", "reasons": "Attributed to al-Khalil; he answers the object-fronting objection by compound particles' changed behavior, comparing هلا. Tabrisi gives phonetic contraction; Alusi reports dropped hamza and alif, with a weak poetic proof. Ibn Ashur approves it."}, {"id": "2:24/q08/p3", "position": "It derives from لا with its alif changed to nūn.", "reasons": "Attributed to al-Farra; Alusi rejects the unmotivated alteration."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q09", "question": "What case does لن govern here?", "turns_on": "Whether cited vowelless verbs show dialectal jussive government or poetic license.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q09/p1", "position": "Normally it makes the imperfect subjunctive, here shown by dropping the plural nūn.", "reasons": "Zajjaj relates the subjunctive to أن and a nounlike clause; Nahhas compares secondary verb cases to noun cases. Wahidi, Tabrisi, Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi concur."}, {"id": "2:24/q09/p2", "position": "Some Arab dialects use لن with a jussive imperfect.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi and Ibn al-Tarawa cite poetry, especially al-Nabigha, and an Ibn Umar dream report. Samin says poetic sukūn explains the evidence instead."}]}

{"id": "2:24/q13", "question": "How are النار and التي parsed, and what forms does التي have?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q13/p1", "position": "النار is the imperative's direct object; التي is its feminine definite relative adjective.", "reasons": "Nahhas, Qurtubi and Samin agree. {"id": "2:24/q14", "question": "Why is the Fire definite and described by a relative clause?", "turns_on": "Whether definiteness points chiefly to prior mention or the Fire's distinctive description.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q14/p1", "position": "It recalls a fire already known, especially the earlier description in al-Tahrim 66:6.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari, Razi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Samin and Burhan contrast a Meccan indefinite mention with this Medinan definite one; some also allow knowledge from the People of the Book or Prophet. Alusi notes that al-Tahrim's priority is disputed. Biqai says the definite report presents divine knowledge as universally established."}, {"id": "2:24/q14/p2", "position": "It identifies a distinctive Fire fueled directly by people and stones.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari and Razi distinguish it from ordinary fires that require initial kindling; Nasafi calls the fuel distinctive, while Abu Hayyan denies that the relative description proves multiple fires."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q15", "question": "What does وقود mean here?", "turns_on": "The initial vowel and whether a noun for fuel can also serve as a verbal noun.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q15/p1", "position": "Fuel or firewood, the material kindling and feeding the Fire.", "reasons": "Most distinguish fatḥa as fuel and ḍamma as burning; Akhfash, Zajjaj, Ibn Jinni, Sibawayh, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Ashur allow overlap or exceptional fatḥa verbal noun. Ibn Ashur says the instrument pattern supports fuel; Samin cites rare fuʿūl verbal nouns, with al-Kisai adding وزوع. Al-Harali says fuel mediates fire's action. Elmalılı includes coal, grass, tinder and rags."}, {"id": "2:24/q15/p2", "position": "It can denote the action of burning or kindling, especially with initial ḍamma.", "reasons": "Akhfash, Ibn Qutayba, Tabari, Zajjaj and later grammarians distinguish the verbal noun; Jishumi compares fiʿl vocalizations. Ibn Jinni adduces وقدت النار وقودا, ولوعا and القبول; his side discussions of وضوء, ساكوت, الضارورة and possessive-yāʾ patterns illustrate irregular formation. Some allow either vowel for both senses."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q16", "question": "Which readings of وقودها are reported?", "turns_on": "Transmission and whether the vowel denotes fuel or burning.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q16/p1", "position": "The prevalent reading has fatḥa on the wāw, matching the fuel sense.", "reasons": "Jishumi calls it general; Ibn Jawzi, Nahhas and Samin prefer it because people and stones are fuel. Ibn Ashur also requires fuel in context."}, {"id": "2:24/q16/p2", "position": "Several readers use ḍamma on the wāw.", "reasons": "Attributed variously to Hasan, Mujahid, Talha, Abu Haywa, Isa al-Hamdani, Isa ibn Umar and Qatada. Ibn Atiyya says Talha excepts al-Buruj; Durr says Mujahid excepts 85:5. Some construe it as verbal noun with ellipsis or intensive identification; Jishumi rejects its recitation, while Alusi says it can be fuel noun."}, {"id": "2:24/q16/p3", "position": "Ubayd ibn Umayr reads وقيدها, also meaning fuel.", "reasons": "Qurtubi records the qaf form; Abu Hayyan identifies a faʿīl pattern; Jishumi rejects it for lack of broad transmission."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q17", "question": "How is وقودها الناس والحجارة parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q17/p1", "position": "It is a nominal relative clause: وقودها is subject, الناس predicate, and الحجارة coordinated with الناس.", "reasons": "Nahhas, Qurtubi and Samin specify the resumptive pronoun. {"id": "2:24/q18", "question": "Who are the people named as fuel?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q18/p1", "position": "Those destined for Hell, particularly disbelievers or sinful people; the general noun is contextually restricted.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan say grammatical generality does not mean every person. {"id": "2:24/q19", "question": "Why mention people before stones?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q19/p1", "position": "People feel pain and are more frightening to see burn; their bodies may also ignite more readily.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Alusi cite sentience, flesh, fat and skin; Ibn Ashur says the pairing indirectly threatens worshippers alongside idols."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q20", "question": "How is الحجارة formed and used in Arabic?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q20/p1", "position": "It is a plural of حجر, often judged irregular beside أحجار.", "reasons": "Wahidi, Jishumi and Ibn Ashur call the plural nonanalogical; Baydawi compares جمالة. {"id": "2:24/q21", "question": "Which stones fuel the Fire?", "turns_on": "Whether the noun denotes a special material, idols, stones as a kind, treasure, or otherwise unknown fuel; the arguments appeal to reports, 21:98, and the threat's intensity.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q21/p1", "position": "Sulfur stones, often described as black, intensely hot, foul, smoky, adhesive, large and hard.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud reports their divine creation as God willed; some place it in the lowest heaven at creation, others in Hell or beneath the second earth. Mujahid says they smell worse than carrion. Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi list five torments; Ibn Kathir cites Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Hakim's authentication and prefers sulfur over idols. Alusi says hadith scholars favor sulfur; Baydawi and Zamakhshari dispute unsupported restriction."}, {"id": "2:24/q21/p2", "position": "Carved idols worshipped alongside God.", "reasons": "Tabrisi, Kashshaf, Baydawi, Ibn Ashur and Tabatabai cite 21:98; idols become punishment and regret after hoped-for intercession fails, analogous to hoarded gold branding its owners at 9:35. Zamakhshari and Tabrisi prefer this; Ibn Kathir calls it weak against sulfur. Biqai includes worshipped idols; Elmalılı includes worshipped structures."}, {"id": "2:24/q21/p3", "position": "Stones generally, showing a fire capable of consuming even rock.", "reasons": "Baghawi and others take no special kind; Mawardi and Tabrisi emphasize its terrifying size and power. Abu Hayyan rejects reducing the clause to mere capability without actual burning. Qushayri argues frail people can endure still less."}, {"id": "2:24/q21/p4", "position": "Heated rocks used to torment sinners, rather than merely a fuel classification.", "reasons": "Tabrisi reports rocks used for torture; Ibn Masud and Ibn Abbas say people are tormented by stones alongside fire. A dark-cloud report says millstone-like rocks rain upon Hell's inhabitants."}, {"id": "2:24/q21/p5", "position": "Hoarded gold and silver.", "reasons": "Baydawi objects that this does not explain why the punishment is specified for disbelievers; Abu Hayyan compares branding hoarders, and Alusi notes a lexical حجر proposal but deems it weak."}, {"id": "2:24/q21/p6", "position": "Unknown otherworldly entities, not ordinary inanimate statues.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu argues punishing inanimate objects would be unjust; it notes that unfamiliar fire could burn unfamiliar stone."}, {"id": "2:24/q21/p7", "position": "Coal or similarly combustible stones.", "reasons": "Elmalılı cites experts in the sciences identifying combustible stone as coal; his broader fuel sense includes ordinary kindling."}]}

{"id": "2:24/q23", "question": "Does mentioning people and stones exclude other beings or imply several fires?", "turns_on": "Whether a distinctive fuel description entails multiple fires.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q23/p1", "position": "It describes one Fire without excluding jinn and devils, who are mentioned elsewhere.", "reasons": "Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Alusi say the named fuel need not exhaust its inhabitants; Abu Hayyan denies that its distinctive description entails multiple fires."}, {"id": "2:24/q23/p2", "position": "Hell has distinct fires, including one fueled by humans and stones and perhaps another by jinn or demons.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari cites the indefinite fire of al-Layl 92:14; Bursevi adduces 66:6 and 92:14 and proposes like-for-like jinn punishment."}]}

{"id": "2:24/q27", "question": "Which variant readings of أعدت are reported?", "turns_on": "Whether the variant substitutes an ʿatād root or makes the preparer explicit.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q27/p1", "position": "أعتدت or iʿtaddat, from عتاد, meaning equipment or provision.", "reasons": "Reported for Abd Allah in Kashshaf, Abu Hayyan and Alusi; Baydawi and Samin record the same sense."}, {"id": "2:24/q27/p2", "position": "Ibn Abi Abla explicitly names Allah as preparer, 'Allah prepared it.'", "reasons": "The reports vary slightly in the exact verb expression but agree on an explicit divine subject."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q28", "question": "Who are الكافرين, and are others also punished in this Fire?", "turns_on": "Whether preparation for disbelievers excludes temporary entry by sinful believers or identifies the chief and permanent recipients.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q28/p1", "position": "Disbelievers as a class, including the addressees and those sharing their disbelief; sinful believers may enter but do not remain forever.", "reasons": "Tabari and Ibn Abbas include comparable disbelief; Wahidi, Tabrisi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi and Bursevi distinguish permanent unbeliever punishment from temporary sinner entry. Qurtubi invokes intercession reports. Alusi says naming the class can censure the addressees, and there is no need to posit another Fire. Biqai includes concealment of signs."}, {"id": "2:24/q28/p2", "position": "This particular stone-fueled Fire is reserved for disbelievers; sinners have another Fire.", "reasons": "Mawardi, Ibn Atiyya, Tabrisi and Qurtubi report it; Tabrisi compares the hypocrites' lowest depth in 4:145. Ibn Atiyya's majority and Abu Hayyan object that sinners also enter the Fire."}, {"id": "2:24/q28/p3", "position": "Disbelievers are the spiritually veiled and cut off from what they seek.", "reasons": "Qashani's inward use of the term connects it to veiling from religion."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q29", "question": "Does أعدت show that Hell already exists?", "turns_on": "Whether the past passive denotes present preparation or a certain future event.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q29/p1", "position": "Yes; something prepared is already created, even if people become its fuel later.", "reasons": "Wahidi says the nonexistent cannot be prepared, Tabrisi compares Paradise and angelic witnessing, and Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi name Mundhir al-Baluti among dissenters. Ibn Kathir cites the Paradise–Fire exchange, Fire seeking relief, eclipse, Night Journey and Ibn Masud's seventy-year falling-stone report. Qurtubi adds the Prophet's visions. Bursevi and Nasafi reject Mu'tazilite or Jahmite denial. Alusi says the completed past is its apparent sense."}, {"id": "2:24/q29/p2", "position": "No; Hell and Paradise will be created later, with 'prepared' expressing a certain future.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan attributes this to many Mu'tazilites, Jahmites and Nujamiyya; Alusi reports the completed-future construal and rejects it as contrary to appearance."}, {"id": "2:24/q29/p3", "position": "Hell exists now but is unfinished; deeds will generate its changing punishments.", "reasons": "People of spiritual unveiling say it presently burns as air without embers while its keepers praise God; human and jinn deeds supply its pains."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q30", "question": "What reports describe Hell's heat, color, depth, and effects?", "turns_on": "The narrations differ in numbers, phenomena, and chains; Ibn Kathir challenges the harmful-things report.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q30/p1", "position": "Hell's fire is far hotter than worldly fire, variously described as one seventieth, and worldly fire was cooled by water or sea.", "reasons": "Abu Hurayra and Abu Said give seventy parts; Anas and Ibn Masud describe twice cooling, and Qashani reports a seventy-times washing variant. Kur'an Yolu cites Bukhari and Tirmidhi."}, {"id": "2:24/q30/p2", "position": "Hell was kindled for three thousand years, becoming red, then white, then black.", "reasons": "Anas attributes this staged report to the Prophet."}, {"id": "2:24/q30/p3", "position": "Hell was kindled for one thousand years at each color stage and now is black and dark.", "reasons": "Abu Hurayra attributes this version to the Prophet; he also says it is blacker than pitch."}, {"id": "2:24/q30/p4", "position": "A falling stone took seventy years to reach Hell's bottom.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud reports the Prophet's explanation of a heard sound; Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir cite Muslim."}, {"id": "2:24/q30/p5", "position": "Every harmful thing is in the Fire, either harmful people or creatures that punish its inhabitants.", "reasons": "Qurtubi gives both interpretations; Ibn Kathir says the report is not preserved or known."}, {"id": "2:24/q30/p6", "position": "A dark cloud rains huge millstone-like rocks on despairing inhabitants and increases the blaze.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports this explanation without an identified transmitter."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q31", "question": "What reports describe the Fire's recipients and prophetic warnings about it?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q31/p1", "position": "The Prophet warned forcefully of the Fire, and worshippers sought refuge when hearing it mentioned.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud recommends refuge in prayer; Abu Layla reports the Prophet's prayer warning; Nu'man describes pulpit repetition that loosened his cloak."}, {"id": "2:24/q31/p2", "position": "Abu Talib's protection benefited him by moving him from Hell's depths to a shallow part.", "reasons": "Al-Abbas asked the Prophet; the Prophet said without his intervention Abu Talib would be in the lowest depth."}, {"id": "2:24/q31/p3", "position": "God fills both Paradise and Fire with those He wills, as mercy and punishment respectively.", "reasons": "Abu Hurayra reports the two speaking to God; Qurtubi cites Bukhari and a Muslim parallel."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q32", "question": "What inward meaning is given to Fire and its fuel?", "turns_on": "The symbolic referents of

 Fire, people, and stones differ.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q32/p1", "position": "Fire is the soul's lower burning turmoil; loved inert things and their embedded images become its fuel.", "reasons": "Qashani cites the saying that a person is gathered with what he loves, even a stone; attachment imprints the heart, and spiritual fire can burn character more deeply than physical fire. Ibn Arabi calls people Hell's flames and idols its embers."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q33", "question": "How does this warning connect to surrounding guidance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q33/p1", "position": "After proof of oneness and prophethood, the threat addresses denial, then the discourse turns to believers' reward.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Abu Hayyan and Wahidi trace the transition; Nasafi says encouragement and warning jointly move conduct; Qushayri says the disbelievers' assigned Fire reassures believers. Kur'an Yolu says revelation calls people away from Fire to mercy and Paradise. Elmalılı notes shifting forms of address."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q34", "question": "Where does the challenge's sentence begin and how does it link to the previous verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the previous verse's صادقين ends a complete unit or the challenge extends into this verse.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q34/p1", "position": "The preceding challenge supplies an understood premise; this verse proceeds from its unanswered demand to its consequence.", "reasons": "Ibn Jawzi makes the premise explicit; Qurtubi reports a complete pause at صادقين for past and future failure, while some commentators continue the challenge through ولن تفعلوا and do not pause there. Samin objects to their construal."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q35", "question": "What is the scope of resurrection implied by human and stone fuel?", "turns_on": "Whether the mention of stones and the sheep report extend recompense beyond the two weighty kinds.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q35/p1", "position": "The pairing implies judgment and recompense across all creation, beyond humans and jinn.", "reasons": "Al-Harali argues stone extends the scope to all in heaven and earth; he says focus on the two weighty kinds is an initial simplification. Biqai cites the report that a hornless sheep receives redress from a horned one."}, {"id": "2:24/q35/p2", "position": "Only humans and jinn are raised for recompense; other creatures receive no reward.", "reasons": "Some scholars interpret the sheep-redress report away, according to Biqai."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q36", "question": "What other theological lessons are drawn from action and punishment here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q36/p1", "position": "Acts imply capable agents, and the Qur'an's challenge is a valid rational proof rather than mere assertion.", "reasons": "Jishumi infers capacity, knowledge and life from acting, awaiting and mediation; Razi rejects the claim that the Qur'an lacks arguments. Elmalılı says persistent doubt after testing comes from obstinacy or self-interest."}, {"id": "2:24/q36/p2", "position": "Punishment fittingly separates what opponents wrongly joined or neglected, prompting restraint through pain.", "reasons": "Al-Harali contrasts restraint guided by knowledge with restraint induced by pain. Biqai supports the fiery-element analogy by 17:27 and 19:83 and says the punished already carry worldly fire in themselves."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q37", "question": "What is the recitational treatment of nūn before lām?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q37/p1", "position": "Retained ghunna before lām depends on whether the nūn remains in the written muṣḥaf.", "reasons": "Al-Dani omits ghunna when the nūn is omitted in writing, citing parallels in Hud and al-Kahf."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q38", "question": "How is the plural verb's alif written?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q38/p1", "position": "An added alif follows plural wāw and remains even when subjunctive or jussive government removes the nūn.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashi explains it as marking the weight of the verbal clause."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q39", "question": "What legal or devotional response is reported on hearing Fire mentioned?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q39/p1", "position": "Seek refuge from Hell during prayer when its verses are recited and ask God for Paradise when it is mentioned.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud recommends this; Abu Layla reports the Prophet doing so while reciting."}, {"id": "2:24/q39/p2", "position": "Ibn Umar disliked using sea water for ablution and preferred dry ablution after contemplating seas set ablaze.", "reasons": "Alusi reports Ibn Umar citing 81:6; it is his reported response, not stated as a universal ruling."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q40", "question": "Does the article in الحجارة denote every stone?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q40/p1", "position": "It denotes the kind of stone involved in the reported fuel, without including every stone.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan distinguishes the article of kind from comprehensive genericity in the specific interpretations of the stones."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q41", "question": "Is the definite article in النار generic?", "turns_on": "Whether definiteness recalls a particular Fire or states a comprehensive kind.", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q41/p1", "position": "It is not generic; it points to a known Fire.", "reasons": "Alusi rejects the generic interpretation while discussing its definite prior description."}, {"id": "2:24/q41/p2", "position": "It is generic or universal, indicating capacity to consume both people and stones.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this from some scholars; the capacity account also appears in Abu Hayyan."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q42", "question": "What is the force of the lām in للكافرين?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q42/p1", "position": "It is an added preposition that makes الكافرين genitive.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas gives this grammatical parsing."}]}
{"id": "2:24/q43", "question": "What practical conclusion follows once the challenge proves revelation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:24/q43/p1", "position": "Belief and Godfearing become obligatory; persistent denial merits Fire, while accepting the Qur'an and Messenger brings deliverance.", "reasons": "Alusi says maximal failure establishes miraculousness and obligation. Razi says the concise threat means abandoning stubbornness after Muhammad's truth is established. Bursevi says inability proves the Messenger and Book and acceptance brings salvation and the Qur'an's merit."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q01", "question": "Who is addressed by the challenge to disbelief?", "turns_on": "Whether address is limited to deniers or extends through admonition.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q01/p1", "position": "All people, including believers, can be warned.", "reasons": "Zajjaj invites believers to marvel; Razi counts four shared blessings, Baydawi permits a mixed or believers-only audience, and Elmalili includes sinners."}, {"id": "2:28/q01/p2", "position": "Disbelievers, especially polytheists.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Tha'labi identify polytheists; Ibn Ashur excludes Jews, who affirm God and resurrection. Baydawi and Abu Hayyan note the turn to direct address."}, {"id": "2:28/q01/p3", "position": "Hypocrites and People of the Book as well.", "reasons": "Tabari addresses professed faith masking denial and Jewish scholars; Qurtubi says rejecting Muhammad and the Quran is denial of God."}, {"id": "2:28/q01/p4", "position": "Prophets, saints, or covenanting believers in inward readings.", "reasons": "Najmiyya applies the address to prophets, saints and Adamic particles answering the covenant."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q02", "question": "What does the opening question do?", "turns_on": "Whether the interrogative is rebuke, wonder, alert or information seeking.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q02/p1", "position": "It rebukes disbelief and denies that it has an excusable state.", "reasons": "Farra compares 81:26; Ibn al-Anbari cites al-Ajjaj; Zamakhshari and later grammarians argue that denying every state entails denying the act. Ibn Ashur asks the disbelievers for an excuse; the imperfect censures persistence."}, {"id": "2:28/q02/p2", "position": "It expresses wonder and asks listeners to marvel.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Qushayri and others stress disbelief despite manifest signs; Burhan and Itqan treat kayfa as an indirect astonishment expression. Divine wonder can mean causing hearers to wonder."}, {"id": "2:28/q02/p3", "position": "It alerts or prompts reflection.", "reasons": "Raghib calls God's kayfa admonitory inquiry; Burhan reports alert rather than wonder."}, {"id": "2:28/q02/p4", "position": "It asks for an account of their state.", "reasons": "Al-Qadi reports this alternative."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q03", "question": "How is kayfa parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether it is termed adverbial or circumstantial.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q03/p1", "position": "It asks about a state and is accusative under takfurun.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, Wahidi, Jishumi, Tabarsi and Raghib contrast state with number, kind, place or essence. {"id": "2:28/q04", "question": "How does kafara govern its object?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q04/p1", "position": "It normally takes bi, though direct government occurs when it means deny.", "reasons": "Samin cites 3:70, 41:41 and 11:68."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q05", "question": "What is the force and scope of the waw clause?", "turns_on": "Whether the circumstantial scope includes future events.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q05/p1", "position": "It is circumstantial, with qad understood before the past verb.", "reasons": "Farra, Tabari and Zajjaj reconstruct wa-qad; examples include 4:90, 12:27, 12:26, 12:45 and 11:42. Wahidi reports Farra's rule for completed past states."}, {"id": "2:28/q05/p2", "position": "The circumstance spans the whole history through return.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari makes present knowledge of past and future the state; Baydawi says proofs confer effective knowledge, and Alusi reports this as an alternative."}, {"id": "2:28/q05/p3", "position": "Only the first life clause is circumstantial; later clauses resume.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan rejects forcing all future clauses into a present state; Samin's Sheikh calls the alternative strained, citing differing forms and conjunctions."}, {"id": "2:28/q05/p4", "position": "It may attach to an implied command to remember.", "reasons": "Biqai proposes this construction."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q06", "question": "How does kana work here?", "turns_on": "How the underlying verb and predicate are explained.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q06/p1", "position": "Kana is incomplete with amwatan as accusative predicate.", "reasons": "Nahhas and Qurtubi parse it; Wahidi and Jishumi also set out complete, extra and implicit-subject uses, comparing 19:29. It marks time in a nominal predication."}, {"id": "2:28/q06/p2", "position": "The noun kaynuna has competing derivations.", "reasons": "Farra treats it as an analogical exception among waw-root verbs; Khalil derives kaywanuna by assimilation and lightening. Farra prefers analogy."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q07", "question": "What was the initial dead state?", "turns_on": "Which pre-life, grave, or primordial event the adjective identifies.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q07/p1", "position": "Lifeless sperm or embryos before ensoulment.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Farra, Qatada and many others locate it in loins or womb; some include clot and morsel. Abu Hayyan prefers womb stages for immediate fa; Ibn Ashur traces elements, food, gametes, clot and morsel. Ibn Masud's Prophetic report gives successive forty-day periods before the spirit. A variant counts semen's departure from the man. Akhfash illustrates predication of former material with a garment as cotton or yarn and an unripe date."}, {"id": "2:28/q07/p2", "position": "People were nonexistent or nothing before creation.", "reasons": "Companion reports and Ibn Atiyya count nonexistence as first death; Ibn Atiyya and Samin prefer it because disbelievers accept the first three stages yet deny resurrection. Alusi contrasts 'you were dead' with God's later causing death."}, {"id": "2:28/q07/p3", "position": "Dust or primal earthly matter.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas through Dahhak traces people to Adam's dust; Razi distinguishes Adam from semen-derived descendants except Jesus. Baydawi and Bursevi include elements and food."}, {"id": "2:28/q07/p4", "position": "Obscurity or being unremembered.", "reasons": "Tabari adduces Arabic usage and Abu Nukhayla's poem, while others cite 76:1 or a verse attributed to Abu Bujayla or al-Mukhabbal. One Ibn Abbas report specifies remembrance through Islam and the Prophet. Tabari prefers obscure embryos later known as humans."}, {"id": "2:28/q07/p5", "position": "The first dead state is ordinary death before grave questioning.", "reasons": "Abu Salih's sequence has life in the grave, another death, then resurrection. Tabari objects that a postmortem audience could not repent; Alusi calls the past-for-future reading remote."}, {"id": "2:28/q07/p6", "position": "It belongs to primordial covenant and extracted Adamic particles.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd invokes 7:172–173, 4:1, 39:6, 4:154 and 5:7; Qurtubi gives expanded counts. Tabari objects that this creates three deaths and lives without an alleged death at extraction; Ibn Kathir calls it unusual."}, {"id": "2:28/q07/p7", "position": "The first death is semen leaving the man's body.", "reasons": "A reported chronology starts with departure from the body, then ensoulment and ordinary death. Tabari says it lacks a trusted interpretive authority."}, {"id": "2:28/q07/p8", "position": "Adam was lifeless clay before receiving spirit.", "reasons": "An attributed account begins at Adam's own formation and extends his life to descendants."}, {"id": "2:28/q07/p9", "position": "It is unmanifest existence within divine knowledge.", "reasons": "Ibn Arabi distinguishes this from ordinary nothingness."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q08", "question": "Is dead literal for matter without prior life?", "turns_on": "Whether dead requires former life, present capacity, or mere absence.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q08/p1", "position": "Yes; dead can mean devoid of life.", "reasons": "Farra and Ibn Qutayba count separated sperm, hair and nails dead; Zamakhshari and Nasafi cite dead town and earth. Abu Hayyan cites 36:33, 41:39, 22:5 and 21:30; Qatada is reported to take it literally."}, {"id": "2:28/q08/p2", "position": "No; for inert pre-life matter it is figurative.", "reasons": "Most cited by Razi and lexicographers require previous life or capacity for life; Razi distinguishes mawāt from mayyit. Zamakhshari compares shared absence of spirit; Ibn Kathir compares dead idols and earth."}, {"id": "2:28/q08/p3", "position": "A developing body capable of life can be called dead properly.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur distinguishes the embryo from permanently inert stuff; Alusi says the decision depends on the definition of death."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q09", "question": "How is amwatan formed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q09/p1", "position": "It is a broken plural of mayyit or its lightened form.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari and Nasafi compare aqwal from qil; Abu Hayyan also includes mayyita and notes expected fa'a'il. {"id": "2:28/q10", "question": "What are life and death as states?", "turns_on": "Whether death is a positive entity and which level of life is intended.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q10/p1", "position": "Life is sensory or animate power; death is its absence or opposite.", "reasons": "Ibn Jawzi connects life with sensation and movement; Baydawi and Ibn Ashur discuss spirit, balanced temperament and embodied faculties. Alusi surveys sensation and equilibrium definitions, noting paralysis and distinct organs; Jishumi calls life an accident only God creates."}, {"id": "2:28/q10/p2", "position": "Life can describe growth, knowledge, faith or renown.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Alusi, Qushayri and Tabari describe figurative senses and corresponding deaths; 57:17 and 6:122 illustrate."}, {"id": "2:28/q10/p3", "position": "Death is absence or privation, not a positive accident.", "reasons": "Abu Hashim denies a death accident; Ibn Ashur says death is nonexistence while life is positive, both created by God."}, {"id": "2:28/q10/p4", "position": "Divine life denotes God's perfection in knowledge and power.", "reasons": "Baydawi allows either predication through associated qualities or a real essential attribute; Alusi speaks of divine perfection."}, {"id": "2:28/q10/p5", "position": "Death is a created positive accident opposed to life.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports the majority citing 67:2."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q11", "question": "What is the first act of giving life?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q11/p1", "position": "God creates and ensouls people for womb and worldly life.", "reasons": "Qushayri describes differentiation into bone, flesh, hair and skin. Damghani says ahya can mean initial creation; Ibn Jawzi compares 3:27, 22:66, 40:11 and 45:26."}, {"id": "2:28/q11/p2", "position": "God makes what was nothing into living humans.", "reasons": "Companion reports stress bringing into being; Abu Hayyan calls it the greatest gift with continued provision and Tabari adds proof of oneness."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q12", "question": "How are the object suffixes parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q12/p1", "position": "Each -kum is an accusative object suffix.", "reasons": "Nahhas parses the suffixes of the three life-and-death verbs as objects."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q13", "question": "How is the first life verb read?", "turns_on": "Whether imala depends on reader or preceding particle.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q13/p1", "position": "Al-Kisa'i inclines it by imala, with or without preceding fa or waw.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid connects alif-prefixed waw roots and compares 91:1 and 93:1; Ibn Khalawayh argues identical pronunciation warrants consistent treatment."}, {"id": "2:28/q13/p2", "position": "Ibn Amir reads the forms open.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid reports complete opening."}, {"id": "2:28/q13/p3", "position": "Hamza inclines comparables after waw but not fa.", "reasons": "Ibn Khalawayh attributes this to ease and heaviness of connected contexts."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q14", "question": "Why fa for the first revival and thumma thereafter?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q14/p1", "position": "Fa marks close succession; thumma marks intervals.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari, Razi, Nasafi and Samarrai distinguish quick first life from later death,

{"id": "2:28/q15", "question": "When does God cause the stated death?", "turns_on": "Which life ends at this stage.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q15/p1", "position": "At the end of worldly life or appointed term.", "reasons": "Tabari describes departure of soul, Qushayri reduction to bones and dust, and Baghawi and Baydawi the appointed lifespan."}, {"id": "2:28/q15/p2", "position": "Again in the grave after questioning.", "reasons": "Abu Salih reports revival and another death; Qurtubi and Kuran Yolu allow this alternative."}, {"id": "2:28/q15/p3", "position": "It is inward death of self or private witnessing.", "reasons": "Sulami, Qushayri and Qashani describe this spiritual stage."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q16", "question": "What is the second life?", "turns_on": "Whether renewed life occurs in grave, at resurrection or inwardly.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q16/p1", "position": "Bodily resurrection for judgment.", "reasons": "Early transmitters place it at the trumpet or Judgment Day; Tabari says restored souls and bodies recognize one another, Biqai says movement is restored, and Razi depicts trumpet, graves and awed silence. {"id": "2:28/q17", "question": "Does the sequence settle life and punishment in the grave?", "turns_on": "Whether the stated count exhausts all stages and how 40:11 relates.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q17/p1", "position": "Silence about grave life does not exclude it; grave punishment is affirmed.", "reasons": "Razi and Abu Hayyan answer the argument from silence. {"id": "2:28/q18", "question": "How does this sequence relate to 40:11?", "turns_on": "Whether the two passages count the same episodes.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q18/p1", "position": "It gives the same two-death and two-life history.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others align 40:11 with pre-world state, first life, worldly death and resurrection. Ibn Kathir compares 45:26, and Kuran Yolu prefers this reconciliation."}, {"id": "2:28/q18/p2", "position": "The primordial covenant supplies another comparison.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd links extraction and pledge to 7:172–173 and other verses; Tabari rejects the extra death it requires."}, {"id": "2:28/q18/p3", "position": "The count does not exhaust exceptional cases.", "reasons": "Hasan, Razi, Abu Hayyan and Qurtubi mention people with more deaths and revivals."}, {"id": "2:28/q18/p4", "position": "The passages count different stages.", "reasons": "Tabatabai contrasts an initial dead condition here with two acts of causing death in 40:11, supporting barzakh; Razi notes the latter is disbelievers' speech."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q19", "question": "What does 'to Him you return' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the destination is judgment, a physical place, resurrection or inward encounter.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q19/p1", "position": "Return to God's judgment and recompense under His authority.", "reasons": "Tabari cites 36:51, Zajjaj 54:8 and 70:43, and Tabarsi compares an affair returning to its governor, excluding spatial movement. Qushayri adds prior decree; Wahidi says divine knowledge and decree determine outcome."}, {"id": "2:28/q19/p2", "position": "Arrival at the place of divine adjudication.", "reasons": "Mawardi, Abu Hayyan and Samin report this gloss."}, {"id": "2:28/q19/p3", "position": "Resurrection or renewed life itself.", "reasons": "Qurtubi compares renewed creation with 21:104; Abu Hayyan reports reference to the earlier revival and helplessness."}, {"id": "2:28/q19/p4", "position": "Return to decree, divine grasp or spiritual witnessing.", "reasons": "Qushayri speaks of decree and grasp; Qashani distinguishes witnessing attributes and vision of essence; Najmiyya gives prophets ascension and saints attraction."}, {"id": "2:28/q19/p5", "position": "Physical movement to a place occupied by God.", "reasons": "Razi names the corporealist reading; he, Abu Hayyan and Alusi reject it because judgment explains the phrase."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q20", "question": "What is the antecedent of ilayhi?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronoun points to God or implied first life.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q20/p1", "position": "God.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya prefers God over resurrection; Abu Hayyan and Samin cite the earlier divine pronouns and supply recompense as implied destination."}, {"id": "2:28/q20/p2", "position": "The earlier revival or its implied helpless state.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Samin report the alternative."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q21", "question": "What does preposing ilayhi accomplish?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q21/p1", "position": "Return is to God alone.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says idols cannot help the deniers at resurrection; Tabarsi names exclusive divine jurisdiction."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q22", "question": "How is turja'un read?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb makes people the agent or leaves God as understood agent.", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q22/p1", "position": "Active: you return.", "reasons": "Ya'qub, with readers listed by Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan, uses intransitive raja'a; Bursevi suggests chosen return, while Ibn Ashur leaves voluntariness unstated. Abu Hayyan says the active loses agency parallelism."}, {"id": "2:28/q22/p2", "position": "Passive: you are returned.", "reasons": "The majority reading, preferred by Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi, preserves God's agency and verse-end cadence; Ibn Ashur says it depicts return despite denial."}]}
{"id": "2:28/q23", "question": "What other recitational detail occurs?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:28/q23/p1", "position": "Ya'qub keeps a final ya at pause and continuation in comparable forms.", "reasons": "Nashr lists farhabun, fattaqun and takfurun."}, {"id": "2:28/q23/p2", "position": "A complete pause follows fa-ahyakum thumma yumitukum.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports Abu Hatim's judgment."}]}
